title: A Learning Culture that Extends Staff Capability
audience: Staff developing or using learning resources; supervisors and managers considering the conditions for voluntary learning, deeper judgment, and useful support across the employee life cycle.

sources.title: One DSD: Building an equity learning culture
One DSD: Inclusive Learning and Knowledge Design

filename: courses/One DSD - A19 - A Learning Culture that Extends Staff Capability.pptx

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
A Learning Culture that Extends Staff Capability
Connect substantive learning, usable resources, feedback, and work conditions so staff can develop understanding and equity practice.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: Learning can help someone understand themselves, examine a difficult question, and act more thoughtfully in their work. Those purposes can reinforce one another without making every reflection produce a report. This course examines how a division supports that learning over time. Fictional DSD service, workplace, and community examples will help you compare resources and practice conditions. The aim is a meaningful learning culture that extends staff capability and access to support, while preserving voluntary participation, private reflection, and actual responsibilities for decisions.

slides.text:
The resource exists, but the question remains
Staff receive a large learning collection. A person needs help explaining a service next step but cannot tell where to begin.

Is the problem missing motivation, a finding route, content depth, or practical fit? The existence of a resource does not answer those questions.
slides.narration: A substantial collection can be valuable and still difficult to navigate at the moment someone needs it. The learner may want a short explanation now and deeper reasoning later. Consider what would help them find the relevant subject and understand how the resource could serve their question. Repeatedly responding with another announcement may leave the same condition unchanged. The case does not establish that the collection is poor or that staff lack interest; it identifies a usable-learning question worth examining.

slides.text:
Capability combines understanding and judgment
Understanding a subject, examining an assumption, comparing options, and recognizing when support is needed are different capabilities.

A learning path can connect them through explanation and practice. It should not become a ranking of employee worth, identity, or intercultural development.
slides.narration: A person may understand a concept and still need practice applying it to an ambiguous service question. Another may benefit from private reflection before deciding what the concept means for them. Both are legitimate learning. The series can offer depth without treating level as rank or assigning a person a developmental position. The useful question is what the subject asks the learner to understand and examine. That keeps the learning substantial while respecting different experiences, purposes, and choices about participation.

slides.text:
Worked example: a service explanation
A: send the same long resource again and ask staff to read it.

B: provide a clear route to the relevant explanation, a realistic practice question, reasoned feedback, and optional deeper reading.

B addresses the learning task. Actual usefulness and later service effects still need examination.
slides.narration: The comparison does not require the long resource to disappear. It asks how a learner reaches the part that matters and has room to examine it. A practical question and feedback can connect explanation with judgment, while deeper reading remains available for more substantial inquiry. This arrangement may be worth examining because it responds to the finding and practice needs together. It does not prove that the person learned or that the service changed. Those are different questions that need fitting evidence.

slides.text:
The resource is sent again
A fictional staff member needs to explain a service next step but cannot find the relevant part of a large collection. The team proposes another general announcement. What is a better inquiry?
A. Assume the staff member does not value equity learning.
B. Identify the finding and learning task, then compare a clearer entry, substantive explanation, and relevant practice with feedback.
C. Delete the deeper material because every resource must be brief.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The collection may contain useful material, but this person cannot reach the part that fits the task. The account does not show lack of interest, and another broad announcement may leave the same difficulty. Compare a clearer route with a meaningful explanation and practice that asks the learner to reason about the service step. Keep deeper material available where it supports the subject. Repeated unclear entry routes can limit who develops capability. The fictional case identifies a design question, not a completed remedy, a learning result, or a finding about the value of the entire collection.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Assume the staff member does not value equity learning.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Identify the finding and learning task, then compare a clearer entry, substantive explanation, and relevant practice with feedback.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Delete the deeper material because every resource must be brief.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The account does not establish disinterest. Repeated motive labels can hide a learning-design barrier. Examine finding, understanding, and practical fit; the learner’s goals and the collection’s full usefulness remain unknown.

Which part needs improvement: finding the subject, understanding it, or using it?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The assumption locates the problem in the learner before examining the route they described. Repetition can make a design barrier appear to be a motivation problem and discourage useful questions. Ask what they needed and where the material became difficult to find. The case supplies no complete account of their goals, prior knowledge, or view of equity learning.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects the response to the task. Repeated unclear routes can restrict capability and service preparation. Compare a useful entry and deeper practice, then examine actual use; a revised resource does not guarantee learning or service improvement.

Which part needs improvement: finding the subject, understanding it, or using it?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response separates the entry route from the depth of the subject. It can support a more usable arrangement without reducing learning to a reminder. Repeated access difficulties may affect preparation for service work, but the effect still needs examination. Compare the actual task and learner account, then keep the revised route’s usefulness and later outcomes open to evidence.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Brevity alone may remove useful reasoning while leaving the route unclear. Repetition can make learning superficial. Compare a concise entry with substantive continuation; the actual need and best arrangement still require inquiry.

Which part needs improvement: finding the subject, understanding it, or using it?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A short entry may help, but deleting depth is not the only response. The learner may need a clear route to substantive reasoning rather than less content. Repeated simplification can leave complex judgment unsupported. Compare formats and purposes before choosing the arrangement. The case does not establish that every resource is too long or that one brief format will meet everyone’s needs.

slides.text:
Findable, understandable, usable
A resource may be hard to find, difficult to understand, or unsuitable at the moment of need. These are different conditions.

Examine which one applies before choosing a response. Shortening every resource may remove useful depth without improving the route to it.
slides.narration: Someone might never reach the correct course because the title uses an unfamiliar term. Another person may reach it and need a clearer explanation. A third may want a deeper account but have a short immediate task. Different supports fit those conditions. A useful learning design can provide a concise entry and substantive continuation rather than force one size for every purpose. Repetition of an unexamined route can make a design problem appear to be a staff attention problem.

slides.text:
Depth stays centered on the subject
Use definitions, distinctions, worked comparisons, and practice that asks the learner to explain a reason. Avoid replacing the subject with generic reminders.

External service delivery and internal culture show why the concept matters. They should deepen the topic rather than distract from it.
slides.narration: A course on bias should help people examine how a judgment forms and how a routine can repeat its effect, not simply remind them to be respectful. A course on access should explain the task and barrier, not rely only on general inclusion language. Relevant examples connect the subject with service decisions and workplace conditions. The learner then has something substantive to practice. That depth can remain clear and warm, with difficult concepts explained in ordinary words rather than made impressive through unnecessary jargon.

slides.text:
Private learning has legitimate value
Reflection can develop personal understanding even when no work product follows. A learner may use fiction rather than disclose private experience.

Do not collect beliefs, identity histories, or inferred developmental positions as proof of learning. Optional resources are not a performance assessment.
slides.narration: Personal understanding is not valuable only when it produces an immediate organizational action. Someone may reconsider a learned meaning or recognize a question they want to explore further. That reflection can remain private. The course should offer a meaningful alternative using fictional examples so learning does not depend on disclosure. Repeated demands to demonstrate personal change can make voluntary learning less safe and less useful. Keep feedback connected to the supplied reasoning and task rather than judging the learner’s identity or inner state.

slides.text:
Learning access is an organizational condition
Consider usable formats, interaction routes, relevant materials, and how learning fits actual work arrangements.

A low participation count does not establish disinterest. Examine conditions and accounts without inventing a permission rule, schedule, or compulsory activity.
slides.narration: Staff may value a topic while finding the material unusable or its place in the work unclear. The relevant question concerns those conditions and the learner’s account, not an assumed motive. Supervisors and managers can discuss support through actual arrangements, but this course does not prescribe a calendar or assign new duties. Repeating the same unsupported learning route may narrow whose capability develops. A better inquiry examines access and fit while preserving voluntary choice and the requirements that already apply to the job.

slides.text:
Feedback explains the reasoning
Name what the response gets right, what assumption or missing condition matters, and how another response could work.

“Good job” and “you do not understand equity” leave different impressions but little guidance. Useful feedback helps the learner reconsider the actual question.
slides.narration: A learner may choose a plausible option that overlooks an important limitation. Feedback should explain that distinction rather than simply mark an answer wrong. For example, a shorter service explanation may be easier to read but omit a condition that must remain accurate. Name both parts and invite another attempt. This kind of response supports judgment without ranking the person. Repeated broad praise or criticism can leave the same reasoning gap untouched, while a specific explanation gives the learner something useful to examine.

slides.text:
The private reflection
A fictional learning activity asks staff to submit a personal identity story so a supervisor can rate growth. The same concept could be examined with a fictional workplace case. What better protects learning?
A. Offer meaningful private reflection and fictional practice, with feedback on case reasoning rather than a personal development label.
B. Require the story because a personal disclosure proves commitment.
C. Remove all reflection because it cannot always be observed as a work product.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A learner can examine an assumption through a meaningful reflection or a fictional case without submitting a private identity story. The activity should teach the subject, not make disclosure a test of commitment. Reasoned feedback can explain what the supplied case response supports and what it misses. It cannot assign an intercultural position or measure the whole person’s growth. Repeated personal ratings may make learning less safe and less useful across onboarding and development. A better design preserves whole-person understanding, optional private reflection, and substantive practice while keeping actual employee records and performance responsibilities separate.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Offer meaningful private reflection and fictional practice, with feedback on case reasoning rather than a personal development label.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Require the story because a personal disclosure proves commitment.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Remove all reflection because it cannot always be observed as a work product.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This preserves whole-person learning and usable practice without coerced disclosure. Repeated personal ratings can burden participation. Give reasoned case feedback and appropriate support; private growth and an intercultural level are not established by the activity.

How can the activity stay substantial without requiring private disclosure or a label?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response keeps the learning purpose substantial while protecting choice. A fictional case can support explanation and feedback on reasoning, and private reflection can remain meaningful without a report. Repeated disclosure requirements may restrict participation or turn learning into an identity assessment. The activity supplies no evidence for a personal developmental label, and it should not be treated as a performance measure.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A disclosure does not prove commitment or authorize a development label. Repetition can make voluntary learning a personal gate. Offer fiction and private reflection; the person’s beliefs and growth remain outside this exercise’s evidence.

How can the activity stay substantial without requiring private disclosure or a label?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: A personal story may be sincere, but it does not establish commitment or give a supervisor a valid growth rating. Requiring it can make the same privacy burden recur across learning activities. Offer meaningful alternatives and focus feedback on the supplied subject and reasoning. The case provides no authority to collect beliefs, infer intercultural positions, or place private reflections in employee records.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Reflection can have legitimate personal value. Removing it may narrow learning to visible products. Preserve a private option and substantive practice; neither reflection nor a work product defines the whole learner’s development.

How can the activity stay substantial without requiring private disclosure or a label?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Reflection can contribute to personal understanding even when no immediate work product follows. Removing it would make visible output the only recognized purpose of learning. Preserve a meaningful private route alongside substantive fictional practice. The learner may choose different purposes, and no single reflection or product measures the whole person. Actual assessment and records boundaries remain important.

slides.text:
The employee life cycle keeps learning connected
Different learning questions arise in recruitment, onboarding, routine assignments, development, supervision, advancement, and transition.

An introductory resource may remain useful while deeper practice is added. Do not assume experienced staff need no learning or that every new employee starts with the same knowledge.
slides.narration: Learning needs can change as the work changes. A new employee may need an introduction to a service term, while an experienced analyst may need to examine its implications in a policy proposal. Both can benefit from clear explanations and relevant practice. The life cycle helps connect these opportunities without assigning knowledge from tenure or rank. Repeatedly offering only introductory material may leave substantive judgment unsupported, while assuming expertise can make clarification difficult to seek. Keep multiple legitimate starting points available.

slides.text:
Learning from community knowledge
Community accounts can reveal a missing question about a service or a different meaning of an explanation. Use them to deepen the subject through appropriate arrangements.

Do not turn one story into a community rule or demand private testimony to make learning relevant.
slides.narration: A person’s account may show that a notice was delivered but the next action remained unclear. That contribution can deepen learning about communication or access without requiring a dramatic story. Preserve the person’s meaning and actual permissions when material informs a course. Different accounts can help learners compare conditions rather than memorize a presumed group preference. Repeated use of a single story as a community template can narrow future judgment. The stronger design teaches learners to ask useful questions and keep differences visible.

slides.text:
Culture briefs prepare the next question
A brief helps learners prepare for respectful inquiry about meaning, participation, and context. It does not describe every person.

Connect the brief with a situation that requires thought. Ask what remains to be learned from the people involved rather than presenting a cultural answer key.
slides.narration: A brief can widen a learner’s awareness and introduce questions they might not have considered. Its value is preparation, not prediction. In a practice case, the learner can ask how a term or invitation may be understood and what the person wants to explain. The case should not reward a stereotype as the correct answer. Repetition of that design could turn learning into a profiling habit. A subject-centered alternative uses the brief to support curiosity while preserving the actual person’s meaning and choice.

slides.text:
A proposed transfer respects actual work
Learning may lead to a draft explanation, a better question, or a comparison of alternatives. Actual policy, service, and publication responsibilities remain.

A practice answer prepares judgment; it does not authorize a change. Guidance can deepen the work without taking it away from staff.
slides.narration: Staff can use learning to prepare a thoughtful contribution within their own responsibilities. An analyst might identify an assumption in a proposal, while another colleague might develop a clearer question for review. These are substantive next steps, not merely attendance. The actual change still follows relevant requirements and authority. Consultation can provide research, analysis, and feedback alongside staff work without becoming a mandatory gate for every use of the resources. The intended direction is growing capability and appropriate support, not dependence on one person to do all equity work.

slides.text:
The One DSD Team shapes the learning
The consultant and One DSD Team examine resources together and decide what belongs in the reduced application for SharePoint.

The Team also chooses Learning Lab topics and who facilitates, within its already established every-other-meeting arrangement. These are shared choices, not new assignments from this course.
slides.narration: The One DSD Team and consultant shape this program together. The consultant introduces the resources, and the One DSD Team examines them together to decide what is useful for the reduced SharePoint application. Learning Labs already have a place every other meeting; the Team chooses the area to explore and whether the consultant or another member facilitates. This course preserves that arrangement rather than inventing another timetable. The learning design supports informed shared judgment about resources, not a top-down list of activities imposed on members.

slides.text:
Community knowledge in a course
A fictional course uses one community account as the correct answer for everyone sharing that identity. The account describes an unclear service route. What is a stronger design?
A. Keep the group answer because it makes the activity easy to score.
B. Avoid community accounts because they cannot establish population results.
C. Preserve the particular account, compare the service condition, and use briefs to prepare questions rather than predict people.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The account offers a service condition and a person’s meaning, which can deepen the subject. Turning it into an answer for every person sharing an identity changes its evidence and teaches a stereotype. A better activity asks the learner to examine the route, consider what remains unknown, and compare practical alternatives. Culture briefs can prepare respectful questions without becoming a cultural answer key. Repeated use of group templates can narrow future service judgment. The contribution should remain within its actual permissions and scope, and no fictional response establishes a real service change or population result.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep the group answer because it makes the activity easy to score.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Avoid community accounts because they cannot establish population results.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Preserve the particular account, compare the service condition, and use briefs to prepare questions rather than predict people.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A particular account cannot establish a group rule. Repeated answer keys of this kind can teach profiling and hide internal variation. Examine the service condition and varied meanings; the community’s shared preference is unknown.

What could the learner examine rather than memorize as a presumed community trait?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Scoring convenience does not justify changing a particular account into a group trait. Repeated use of that design may train learners to expect the same meaning from everyone and overlook a different actual need. Preserve the account’s scope and examine the condition it describes. The service route, individual meaning, and possible alternatives are substantive questions without a stereotyped answer key.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Limited accounts can still deepen learning. Removing them may erase useful service knowledge. Keep their scope and combine them with a meaningful question; neither population prevalence nor a universal cause is established.

What could the learner examine rather than memorize as a presumed community trait?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An account does not need to establish a population result to teach something useful. Its particular meaning can help learners notice a condition a general reminder misses. Removing it may narrow whose knowledge informs the course. Preserve scope and permissions, pair it with an appropriate question, and keep broader prevalence and universal cause unestablished.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This keeps community knowledge substantive and bounded. A recurring unclear route can be examined without stereotyping. Compare meanings and practical alternatives, preserving permissions; no account establishes everyone’s experience or a proven remedy.

What could the learner examine rather than memorize as a presumed community trait?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response keeps the subject and the person’s contribution central. It teaches learners to examine a practical condition while respecting different meanings within a community. A brief supports preparation, not prediction. Alternatives still need fitting evidence, and actual use of an account must follow permissions. The learning case does not establish everyone’s experience or a completed service improvement.

slides.text:
Choose resources for fuller course development
The consultant and One DSD Team also decide which e-learning resources should become full Articulate 360 courses for DHS Pathlore.

Consider subject purpose, depth, practice, and learner use. Selection is a development choice; it does not imply that conversion or agency approval has already occurred.
slides.narration: Some resources may serve well as a concise tool, while others deserve a fuller learning experience. The shared review can consider which subjects need explanations, examples, feedback, and deeper practice for end users. Selected courses are intended for development in Articulate 360 and delivery through Pathlore. Choosing a candidate does not mean the course has already been converted or approved. Preserve those distinct stages and the Team’s shared decision rather than turning every resource into an automatic development assignment.

slides.text:
Rewrite a learning purpose
Choose a subject and complete two thoughts: what the learner should understand, and what question they should be able to examine.

Connect a service and workplace example where useful. Keep personal reflection legitimate without requiring a report or a prescribed action from every learner.
slides.narration: Try writing a learning purpose that is specific enough to guide the material. For example, understanding a communication assumption is different from memorizing a reminder to respect people. The second thought might ask how that assumption affects a service route or an employee opportunity. These connections should fit the topic rather than become a checklist pasted into every slide. The reflection can remain private and use fiction. Its value is a clearer purpose that supports substantive teaching and thoughtful practice.

slides.text:
Examine learning and work conditions separately
A reasoned practice response can show how a learner approaches the supplied case. Actual service use and workplace conditions require their own evidence.

Keep the inquiry useful and proportionate. Do not infer a private belief or assign an intercultural level from a course response.
slides.narration: A practice response can reveal that a learner distinguished an observation from an assumption in this case. That is useful feedback about the supplied reasoning. It does not explain the person’s whole development or establish a change in actual service access. Those questions need different evidence. Keep learning assessment focused on what it can support and organizational inquiry focused on actual conditions. This distinction makes the series more serious about capability while protecting learners from labels that the exercise cannot justify.

slides.text:
Keep the resource connected to current work
Review subject accuracy, source changes, user questions, and practical fit through the responsibilities already in place.

A resource can remain valuable while needing revision. Do not let familiar wording become permanent when the relevant work or evidence has changed.
slides.narration: Sustained learning includes attention to how the resource continues to serve people. A policy term may change, a link may no longer lead to useful information, or learners may identify an assumption in a case. Those are reasons to examine the material, not evidence that the whole program failed. The appropriate maintenance responsibilities still need to be followed. A useful update preserves subject depth and acknowledges what changed, helping the next learner connect the resource with current understanding and actual work.

slides.text:
Learning that strengthens independent practice
Substantive explanation, relevant practice, usable access, and guidance can help staff deepen understanding and examine equity within their responsibilities.

The program extends support across the division while preserving shared learning choices, private reflection, and actual decision processes.
slides.narration: A learning culture grows through meaningful opportunities to understand and practice, alongside conditions that make those opportunities usable. The program can extend support beyond a single consultation by giving staff resources they can return to independently or with colleagues. The consultant remains available for substantive guidance, while the Team helps shape the learning collection. Consider one resource in your own work and ask which part would help a learner think more deeply. A thoughtful improvement can strengthen capability without prescribing the same journey or outcome for everyone.

outcomes: Compare learning options against a meaningful purpose and learner needs.
Connect understanding, practice, feedback, and a considered next step.
Identify barriers to learning opportunities across the employee life cycle.
Explain how shared resource choices support personal growth and practical equity work.
